title: Albert Einstein
summary: German-born theoretical physicist who reshaped the understanding of space, time, gravity and light, and received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics.

age6_8.summary: A scientist who worked out surprising things about space, time and light.
age6_8.body:
Albert Einstein was a scientist. He was born a long time ago, in 1879 [1].

He thought very hard about light, and about time, and about why things fall down.

He worked out something surprising: time does not tick at the same speed everywhere. It goes very slightly slower when you move fast [2].

He also said that heavy things bend space, and that is what gravity really is [2].

He won a big prize called the Nobel Prize [1].

He had wild white hair, and lots of people know his face.

age9_12.summary: The physicist whose ideas about relativity changed how we understand space, time and gravity.
age9_12.body:
Albert Einstein was a theoretical physicist — a scientist who works out how nature behaves using maths and reasoning rather than experiments [1].

## An unpromising start

Einstein struggled to find an academic job after university. In 1905 he was working as a clerk in the Swiss patent office in Bern [1].

That year, in his spare time, he published four papers. Any one of them would have made a career. Together they changed physics. Historians call it his *annus mirabilis* — miracle year [2].

## Special relativity

Einstein started from a strange fact: light always travels at the same speed, no matter how fast you are moving.

If that is true, something else has to give. Einstein showed it is time and distance themselves. Clocks moving quickly tick more slowly, and moving objects shrink slightly along the direction of travel [2].

This is not an illusion. Satellite navigation systems must correct for it or they would give wrong positions [2].

From this came E = mc²: mass and energy are the same thing in different forms.

## General relativity

Ten years later Einstein extended the idea to gravity. Instead of a force pulling across empty space, he proposed that mass bends space and time, and things simply follow the bent shape [2].

The theory predicted that starlight passing the Sun would be deflected. This was measured during a solar eclipse in 1919, and Einstein became world-famous almost overnight [2].

## Later life

Einstein was Jewish. When the Nazis came to power in 1933 he left Germany and settled in the United States, where he worked at Princeton until his death in 1955 [1].

He won the 1921 Nobel Prize — but for explaining the photoelectric effect, not for relativity [1].

teen.summary: Theoretical physicist whose 1905 and 1915 work established special and general relativity and helped found quantum theory.
teen.body:
Albert Einstein (1879-1955) was a theoretical physicist whose work fundamentally revised the concepts of space, time, mass, energy and gravitation [1].

## 1905: the miracle year

While employed as a patent examiner in Bern, Einstein published four papers in a single year [2]:

**The photoelectric effect** — proposing that light is quantised into discrete packets. This contributed directly to the founding of quantum mechanics and was the work cited in his 1921 Nobel Prize [1].

**Brownian motion** — explaining the jittering of suspended particles as the result of molecular collisions, providing strong evidence that atoms are real, which was still disputed.

**Special relativity** — resolving an incompatibility between Maxwell's electromagnetism and Newtonian mechanics by taking the constancy of the speed of light as a postulate.

**Mass-energy equivalence** — the short follow-up paper giving E = mc².

## Special relativity

The theory rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are identical in all inertial frames, and the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers regardless of their motion.

Holding these together requires abandoning absolute simultaneity. Time dilation, length contraction and the relativity of simultaneity follow as consequences. These are not perceptual effects but properties of spacetime, and they are routinely confirmed — the lifetimes of fast-moving muons, and the relativistic corrections required by satellite navigation, are direct measurements [2].

## General relativity

Einstein spent a decade extending relativity to accelerated frames and gravitation, completing the general theory in 1915. Its central insight, the equivalence principle, is that being at rest in a gravitational field is locally indistinguishable from acceleration.

The theory recasts gravity as spacetime curvature sourced by mass-energy. It resolved the long-standing anomaly in Mercury's perihelion precession and predicted gravitational deflection of starlight [2].

Arthur Eddington's 1919 eclipse expedition reported deflection consistent with the prediction. The result was reported worldwide and made Einstein a public figure in a way no scientist had been before.

## Quantum mechanics and later work

Despite his foundational contribution to quantum theory, Einstein was never reconciled to its probabilistic interpretation. His 1935 EPR paper with Podolsky and Rosen argued quantum mechanics must be incomplete. It was intended as a critique, but it identified entanglement — and later experimental tests of Bell's inequalities have supported quantum mechanics over the local-realist position Einstein preferred [2].

The paper is now regarded as among his most influential, for reasons opposite to those he intended.

## Public life

Einstein left Germany permanently in 1933 following the Nazi seizure of power, taking a position at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton [1].

In 1939 he signed a letter to President Roosevelt warning that Germany might develop nuclear weapons — a letter that helped initiate the Manhattan Project. Einstein took no part in the project itself and later described signing it as a serious mistake. He spent his final years advocating for nuclear disarmament and civil rights [1].

adult.summary: Theoretical physicist (1879-1955) whose special and general theories of relativity restructured classical physics, and whose light-quantum hypothesis contributed foundationally to quantum theory.
adult.body:
Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist whose work constitutes one of the two principal reorganisations of twentieth-century physics, the other being quantum mechanics — to which he also contributed decisively, and with which he remained in unresolved disagreement [1].

## Annus mirabilis, 1905

Working as a technical expert at the Swiss Federal Patent Office and holding no academic position, Einstein published four papers in the *Annalen der Physik* in 1905 [2].

The light-quantum paper proposed that electromagnetic radiation is quantised, explaining the frequency threshold of the photoelectric effect that classical wave theory could not accommodate. This was the work for which the 1921 Nobel Prize was awarded — relativity being considered insufficiently confirmed at the time [1].

The Brownian motion paper derived quantitative predictions for the displacement of suspended particles from molecular kinetic theory, providing an experimentally testable case for atomic reality at a time when it remained contested.

The electrodynamics paper introduced special relativity. The mass-energy paper followed, establishing equivalence of mass and energy.

## Special relativity

Special relativity proceeds from two postulates: covariance of physical law across inertial frames, and invariance of the vacuum speed of light. Their joint acceptance requires abandoning absolute simultaneity, yielding time dilation, length contraction and the relativistic velocity addition law, unified in Minkowski's four-dimensional geometric formulation.

The theory is among the most stringently tested in physics. Muon lifetime dilation, relativistic Doppler measurements, particle accelerator kinematics and the relativistic corrections required for satellite navigation all confirm it to high precision [2].

## General relativity

The general theory, completed in 1915, extends covariance to arbitrary coordinate systems and incorporates gravitation. The equivalence principle — the local indistinguishability of gravitation and acceleration — motivates identifying gravity with the geometry of spacetime, and the Einstein field equations relate curvature to the stress-energy tensor.

The theory accounted for the anomalous perihelion precession of Mercury, a discrepancy unexplained since 1859, and predicted light deflection at twice the Newtonian value. Eddington's 1919 eclipse observations reported agreement, and Einstein achieved a level of public celebrity unprecedented for a scientist [2].

Subsequent confirmations include gravitational redshift, Shapiro delay, frame dragging, binary pulsar orbital decay, direct gravitational-wave detection from 2015, and horizon-scale black hole imaging from 2019.

## Quantum mechanics and the EPR argument

Einstein's relationship with quantum mechanics is frequently misrepresented. He was not a sceptic of the theory's predictive success, which he had helped establish; he rejected the claim that its probabilistic description is complete.

The 1935 paper with Podolsky and Rosen argued that quantum mechanics either permits nonlocal influence or is incomplete. Bell's 1964 theorem rendered the disagreement experimentally decidable, and subsequent Bell tests have consistently favoured quantum mechanical predictions over local hidden-variable theories.

Einstein's conclusion has not been sustained; his identification of entanglement as the crux has proved foundational to quantum information science [2].

## Later career and public role

Einstein emigrated permanently in 1933, joining the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton. His later research pursued a unified field theory and did not succeed; the programme was widely regarded as isolated from the main development of physics at the time.

In 1939 he co-signed the letter to Roosevelt warning of the possibility of German nuclear weapons, contributing to the initiation of American nuclear research. He held no role in the Manhattan Project and subsequently characterised the letter as a mistake. He devoted much of his remaining public life to nuclear disarmament, and spoke publicly against racial segregation in the United States [1].
